abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel theoretical framework termed "Physics-Informed Implicit Neural Representation (PI-INR)" for biomedical image reconstruction, fundamentally challenging conventional model-based and learning-based paradigms. Unlike existing approaches that rely on explicit parameterization of imaging physics, PI-INR encodes the complete forward model as an implicit neural network function, enabling continuous and resolution-independent representation of imaging data. We establish the theoretical foundations by proving universal approximation bounds for inverse problems solved through implicit differentiation, demonstrating that the proposed framework possesses superior regularization properties compared to traditional compressed sensing methods. The mathematical analysis reveals that PI-INR naturally incorporates prior knowledge through differentiable physics constraints, achieving theoretically optimal sample complexity for limited-angle CT and accelerated MRI reconstruction. Extensive experiments on synthetic phantoms and clinical datasets demonstrate that PI-INR outperforms state-of-the-art methods by up to 3.2 dB in PSNR while reducing computational complexity by an order of magnitude. This work establishes a new paradigm for medical image reconstruction that unifies neural network representation with physics-based modeling, opening promising research directions for image-guided therapy and quantitative imaging analysis.

This paper presents a significant theoretical advancement in multi-modal medical image registration by developing a unified information-theoretic framework that generalizes classical similarity measures. We derive a novel family of entropy-based metrics, denoted as "Adaptive Mutual Information Gradient (AMIG)", which dynamically adapts to local image statistics and tissue characteristics. The theoretical analysis establishes that AMIG satisfies crucial mathematical properties including symmetry, uniqueness, and robustness to intensity inhomogeneities inherent in MRI and CT acquisitions. We prove convergence guarantees for gradient descent optimization using AMIG as the objective function, demonstrating a 40% reduction in optimization iterations compared to conventional normalized mutual information. The proposed framework incorporates a learned attention mechanism that automatically weights voxel contributions based on structural saliency, enabling more accurate alignment of anatomical landmarks. Validation on diverse datasets including brain MRI, cardiac CT, and whole-body PET-CT shows that AMIG achieves sub-voxel registration accuracy with 28% improvement in target registration error over existing methods. This work provides rigorous theoretical foundations for next-generation computer-aided diagnosis systems requiring precise multi-modal image fusion.

We present "MedVision-Transformer" (MVT), a novel end-to-end system architecture for real-time ultrasound image analysis that integrates acquisition, processing, and diagnostic interpretation within a unified framework. The system introduces a hierarchical vision transformer with localized self-attention mechanisms specifically designed for the unique noise characteristics of ultrasound imaging, including speckle noise and acoustic shadow artifacts. The MVT architecture employs a multi-scale feature extraction pipeline that simultaneously processes beamformed radio-frequency data and post-processed B-mode images, enabling unprecedented integration of raw and processed medical imaging information. Key system innovations include a learned beamforming module that replaces traditional delay-and-sum methods, a novel tissue-specific normalization layer, and an interpretable attention-based diagnostic head that generates spatially-precise abnormality heatmaps. The complete system operates at 45 frames per second on embedded GPU hardware, meeting real-time requirements for image-guided therapy applications. Clinical validation with 2,847 patients demonstrates that MVT achieves radiologist-level accuracy in detecting fetal anomalies, thyroid nodules, and cardiac dysfunction, with an average AUC of 0.94 across all diagnostic tasks. This paradigm shift from sequential processing to integrated intelligent imaging represents a transformative approach for medical visualization and computer-aided diagnosis.

This paper introduces an improved deep learning system for automated medical image segmentation in MRI, addressing critical limitations of U-Net architectures in handling anisotropic voxel resolutions and variable anatomy sizes. The proposed "Adaptive Scale Fusion Network" (ASF-Net) incorporates a novel multi-scale attention mechanism that dynamically adjusts receptive fields based on local anatomical context, eliminating the need for manual slice thickness standardization. The system architecture features a cascaded design with three stages: coarse localization, scale-adaptive refinement, and boundary-sensitive prediction, each optimized through dedicated loss functions promoting volumetric consistency. A key innovation lies in the learned inter-slice interpolation module that enables accurate 3D segmentation from sparsely sampled MRI slices, reducing acquisition time by 60% while maintaining diagnostic quality. The system includes an uncertainty quantification module that generates confidence maps for clinical decision support, addressing interpretability requirements in computer-aided diagnosis. Evaluated on multi-institutional MRI datasets encompassing brain tumors, cardiac structures, and abdominal organs, ASF-Net demonstrates consistent improvements of 4.1% in Dice coefficient and 18% reduction in Hausdorff distance over current state-of-the-art methods. The system has been deployed in clinical workflow for automated quantification in radiology departments.
